sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay. Today is June 11, 2002. I am Gail Lowery with Senator Lugar's office. And I'm here today with Mr. John H. Flack at Home Place in Carmel, Indiana. And, Mr. Flack, if we could just have you start with your -- the branch of service you were in and what war, rank, and where you served, sir.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: I was in the United States Marine Corps, and I served during World War II. I went through boot camp March 25 till -- of '44 until May of '44. And after that, after boot camp, I had three months of armoured amphibious assault tactics and maneuvers and some classroom schooling, but most of it was with the amtracks.
An amtrack is an armoured amphibious assault unit. It weighs fifteen to seventeen tons, 25-foot long, 10-foot wide, 10-foot high with three machine guns and a crew of four.

And after -- when I went overseas in the Fall of 1944, I stopped at Pearl Harbor. And then on to the New Hebrides Islands to pick up some Australian and New Zealand troops who was on the ship with us, troop ship, and on to Guadalcanal.

And we came up to Guadalcanal and there was close to five hundred of us left. And two hundred and fifty approximately went to the 6th Marine Division, which is stationed on Guadalcanal. And we was there several days and my older brother, Perry, was killed in action off Guadalcanal on November 13 of 1942. His ship was very severely damaged and I thought he may be buried in the Marine Corps and Navy cemetery; however, I visited the cemetery and he was not on the roll.

From there we boarded the -- a smaller ship and we went about sixty miles northwest of Guadalcanal to the Russell Islands and to the Island of Pavuvu. Pavuvu is where the 1st Marine Division was stationed and I joined the 1st Amtrack Battalion, which is armoured amphibious assault.

And we were immediately preparing for the invasion of Okinawa and we went on maneuvers and prepared ourselves for the invasion, which subsequently happened on April the 1st, 1945, which was also Easter Sunday and April Fool's Day. And the code -- the code name for the operation -- for the P.D. landing was "love day" L-O-V-E; however, our gunnery sergeant said, "The first one of you guys calls this love," he says, "I'll put my Number 10 boot where" -- he said we're going to be killing them and they'll be killing us and there will be a lot of good American boys die." And he says, "I don't want to hear the word 'love'," which we understood.

And to backtrack a little -- well, to -- we went ahead and hit Okinawa -- but on the third wave and we carried Marines to two -- two squadron marines and -- two squadron marines on an amtrack or -- our amtrack, we carried two thousand pounds or two -- we carried two ton, excuse me, of high explosive shells and demolition equipment. And we reached the third wave and they estimated we would have eighty percent losses; however, we walked ashore almost with dry boots. The Japs were on another part of the island.

We found a whooping party there, but we -- we came in and found the artillery regiment and they took the explosives and the ammunition off and ordinarily we go back out there out to the troop ship and bring in more, but in this case we were ordered to stay with the infantry as they advanced and we did. And we went over to, close to the 6th Marine Division. They were battling Yontan Airfield and part of that was our responsibility, so we went in with them and fought with them. And it took about an hour and a half to two hours to take the Yontan Airfield, which was really scheduled to having to take three days. And we -- there was wounded and we evacuated the wounded in our amtrack back out to what we call L.S.T. hospital ship.

They took an L.S.T., which ordinarily carries tanks and amtracks and heavy equipment. Their deck -- the deck of the L.S.T. can hold one hundred cots. And so what they would do, they never did it before, prior in the Pacific, the L.S.T. would come right up to the shore of the beach and we could just take them from the battlefield straight through right on the L.S.T. and within minutes they were being given medical care.

And then we went back quickly. We stayed with the infantry a couple of hours, having a couple of fire fights with snipers. And then we were ordered back -- our battalion was ordered back to where the beach head was and we were given the responsibility, along with a company of Marines, to have the beach defense, because ordinarily, historically, the Japs counter-attacked the night of the -- of our first day on the beach

So we dug in, put machine gun in placement, and the infantry -- we stayed -- they intermingled among us. We had three machine guns for each amtrack and our battalion had a hundred of them, so we had plenty of fire power. And so it took us about half an hour, forty-five minutes before darkness and we just remembered we hadn't eaten all day. So we, out with the c-rations and one of the boots, of which I was also one, built a fire to heat a c-ration. They said, "No, it's going to be dark. You know, why guide the Japs in."

So that's fine. So we opened up the c-rations and one of the guys turned on the radio and we got Tokyo Rose. And she was -- we could hear her saying that the 1st Marine Division, all are dead, just by the thousands laying on the beach. All of your ships are sunk and airplanes are shot down and the Japanese control the beach and all that. Now, we couldn't see a Jap. So anyhow, and then she played some music. And as the war went on, we got Tokyo Rose quite a bit and we looked forward to hearing from her because she had up-to-date music; Glen Miller and things like that. And people say, well, she should be executed because it endangered our morale. It never bothered us a bit. We knew what we are, which is Marines. And we knew what to do because we had been trained for and we knew we had to get the war over so we could go home.

And if I can advance a little bit, when they did apprehend Tokyo Rose, they put her on trial, and they said the only reason they didn't execute her because she was a Japanese citizen, but did live in America. But we said if they was going to do that, all the Marines were going to be character witnesses for her. And perhaps those who were never in the war or never in that theater of war would never understand.
But anyhow, why --

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Now, let me -- let's back up just a minute and then you can -- just by way of getting a little bit of history. I'm going to read you a couple of questions and then I'll just let you answer them.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Yes, ma'am.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Were you drafted or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: I enlisted.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: And where were you living at the time?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Yes. I was with mom and dad.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: So you enlisted?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: And I enlisted.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Yes, ma'am.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay. What city and town?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Indianapolis, downtown.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay. And why did you pick the branch of service that you joined?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Well, my marine buddies will kill me, but actually three of us went -- three of my buddies -- two of my buddies and I went down to join the Navy, but the line was so long in the Federal Building they said it would be six weeks if he signed us up that day. And we said, well -- he said, "Do you think you guys" -- this Navy chief was talking to us and he says, "Do you think the war is going to pass you by?" And we said, "Yes," you know. What did we know. And he said, "Would you like to go where there's no lines in the hallways, no recruits in their office, and they sign you up right away?" And we said, "Yes, sir." And he said, "Try the Marine Corps." That should have told us something.

So we went down to Pennsylvania and Washington Street up on the second floor, that's where the Marine Corps recruiting was and we came in the office, there was nobody there. And we walked in and they said, "Boy, just what we need. Have you got any papers on you?" Well, we had our birth certificates and all of that, which I had altered mine. And I used ink eradicator, which I had a ton of it on the -- I marked out my real date of birth and put where I was a year older. And the Sergeant looked at it and he said, "Just what we're looking for. Kid, you're going to be a sergeant out of boot camp." I'm still waiting. I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: No, you're great. Just keep telling the story. It's wonderful. Why don't you tell me about your first days in the service and what it felt like and if you remember any of your instructors, that kind of thing.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Well, of course, it's the Marine Corps. They're much different than other branches. And, of course, the Marine Corps thinks we're the best and I cannot tell a lie, we are. And so anyhow, after we took our physicals and I had a problem there. I was only sixteen. And we went down to the armory on 1400-1500 South Meridian and we stripped down to nothing and they put a number on us. And there was not only doctors examining us, but there was nurses running in, in between, you know. You know, I was a little young.

So anyhow, finally we got papers to carry from desk to desk. Well, that helped me. But anyhow, pretty soon we got used to it. But anyhow, so we passed our physicals and all that, were sworn in, and told us they would call us. Well, they did. And we boarded a train and headed for San Diego, California. And there was a few -- quite a few of us from Indianapolis, but there was other marines-to-be all the way from Buffalo, New York. And then they put an Army first sergeant in charge of us to see that, you know, we didn't get out of hand and things like that.

And a few of the older guys brought booze with them. And the first sergeant, he tolerated -- he had been in many, many years. But, you know, he said, "If you get out of hand, you know, you're in trouble." And so -- then he came along and checked our identification and all of that to make sure we should be there. And/or if we didn't have what was needed, he would note it. And when he got to me and he looked at me and he said, "How long have you been dodging the draft, old timer?"

Anyhow, so on the train we had good times and then we got out West and for the first time I found the Harvey Restaurants, they were made a show about it later on with Judy Garland, "The Harley Girls." And we had priority because we were on the way to go fight the war and win it. And all of us in civies and most of us young, there were a couple of old guys on there in their twenty-eight to thirty years old, sad.

And so when we pulled up like out West, you know, why other people waiting in line, you had servicemen waiting in line. They were on their way to furlough or something, you know, they were on the train for some reason or another. And so they take us right around and feed us first and then, you know, they didn't like that and they voiced themselves. By that time they picked up a marine sergeant and he said, "I want you to know that these guys are going to be fighting Marines in a couple of months and overseas and fighting for your country." Well, all the civilians applauded, but the guys who were in the service, all they said is, "You'll be sorry."

So we arrived at boot camp and we arrived at Los Angeles and then got on the train down to San Diego. And then from there they put us in buses and up to the Marine Corps Training Temple. And we all fell out, you know. And so that -- a couple of drill instructors said -- it was 2:00 in the morning. He said, "Get a good night's sleep tonight and reveille is at 05:00 and you better be up and you better be ready and you better be shaved, showered," and all of that, you know.

Not many of us slept the first night. So anyhow -- but we made it and we -- they ran us over to the chow line. We still had civies on and all of that stuff, you know. And then after that we went over to the hospital and had another complete physical. They didn't reject anybody that I know of. But anyhow, after that then we went to the Quarter Master and we receive dark dungarees and all of that. Now, we felt like marines then, but you're not allowed to wear the marine ornament in boot camp. You have to earn it. And you had to button your collar up here all the way. And -- so anyhow, after that got taken care of and then they called us out in formation and then they start telling us when the -- from the tallest to the front down to where I was at, you know.

The little guy my size in the Marine Corps is called a feather merchant. And when you march you always get in the tail end and it's dust -- you're dusty. And you got a whole platoon running either fast or whatever and you've got to run, you've got to go slow, all that stuff.

But anyhow -- so this -- P.F.C. Lambert went over there, one of our drill instructors come out and he was mean. He was about 6'2", 6'3", big Alabama boy. And he told us that you're lower than dirt and this and that and things like that. And he said then, "One thing I want you to know, if you do not learn to hate me by three days I'm not doing my job." And we said, "Yes, sir." Everyone was, "Yes, sir." The only person you could speak to in boot camp without asking permission and waiting till they give you permission is your fellow boot. And so after three days, why Lambert -- we fell out, you know, and got in formation and Lambert says -- he says, "Well, three days is up. Have you learned to hate me in three days?" And a couple of guys said, "No, sir." And he said, "What do you mean? Give me an explanation, Boot." He said, "It only took two days, sir." Around the grind, around the whole parade field until we was dropping, you know. Then you learned when to keep your mouth shut.

So we went on, went through the different things and all of that. And then we went up to the rifle range after about five weeks, six weeks, and we fired on the range. I didn't do as good as I wanted to, but I qualified. But my instructor told me, he said, "Kid, I'm going to tell you something." He said, "I'm going to say you're not a good shooter," he says, "but you better have your bayonet ready." And, "Yes, sir. Yes, sir." And then after that we came back and things kind of slacked down. Well, they interviewed us and what we wanted to go into. Well, I was sixteen and he said, "Tell me about your experience and your background." I says, "I don't know if I have one." And I said, "Well, I did work for six months for an Army Air Corps depot at" -- well, am I interfering -- excuse me --

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: So anyhow, I had worked -- I left high school as a sophomore. I knew I was going to go in either the Navy or Marines. So anyhow, he said, "Did you do any work anywhere?" And I said, "Oh, yes, the Army Air Corps depot at the state fairgrounds there in Indianapolis." And he said, "What did you do there?" And I said, "Well, they taught me how to ride a" -- I can't think of the name. It's got levers and things like that. Anyhow -- forklift. Yeah, a forklift.

And he says, "How's that operate?" And I said, "Well, you've got your levers. You go hm-um, like that." Well, that's how you drive a tank or an amtrack. And he says, "Any other part of the Marines you would like to be in?" I said, "Yeah, I would like to be a radio gunner in the Marine Corps." He says, "I don't know. Your record on the Marines doesn't qualify you." And he said, "But why do you want to be one for?"

Well, I didn't really tell him down deep I could just see myself getting those golden wings and a gal on each shoulder. That's the way -- you know. Kissed once. Twice, my mother kissed me, too. So anyhow, he says, "Well, we'll let you know," and all that. And I said, "I'll go anywhere you want me to go." And he said, "Okay, kid." So they put me in amtracks and I went through the training and all that three months.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: All in California?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Yes, Oceanside, California, which is straight across the street from Camp Pendleton, because we had to be near the beach. And we had an incident. We was there about a month or six weeks in our amtrack training and every time we got a new guy in our class we would initiate him. Once we get out past the breakers, the surf, we toss them in, you know. You know, we were old timers. We had six weeks.

Anyhow, so this one day we went out, you know, and we had an instructor, a corporal. And he didn't even see that we got a new guy, but we did. And he looks older than us. In fact, he had a little gray hair, a big hawk nose, brand new dungarees, brand new everything. So we thought he just got out of the brig, you know. So we were going to pick that old guy.

And so we get out beyond the breakers and then he lights up a cigarette, which is a no-no. I mean, that's death or you'll be shot at dawn, you know, because we had a hundred and ten gallons of high test gasoline. And he lit a cigarette and the instructor didn't even say anything. He was always screaming at us, for good reason. And so we went out, you know, beyond the breakers and, boy, we go up there and grab him and one, two -- and just as we was tossing him, the corporal yelled, "Captain, Captain." We threw a captain into the brink.

We were both privates. We didn't even have six months in the Marine Corps yet. He didn't have good words for us. But this old guy, we gave him the boat hook and got him out of the water. He still had that ______ cigarette, you know. And he said, "Well, I guess that makes me one of the boys." So the corporal quieted down. And we got to know him. And he was quite a hero with the Marine Corps. He got the Navy Cross, which is next to the Medal of Honor, during the battle from Makin Island with Carlson's Raiders. And I don't know whether you're familiar with the raiders in the Marine Corps, but it's like the Rangers are with the Army and the Seals are with the Navy.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Except we were the first ones to have them. Well, this man was machine gunned real bad and still did what was supposed to be done and they never did evacuate him till the fighting was over. And the Navy I think and two hundred marines by boat, way out in the islands, next to the Gilbert Islands, not far from Tarawa. So they -- what they did, they blew up this and that and the other thing and their radio stations and -- but anyhow, he got to where -- when we would get off duty, we would go to what we call a swap shoot. That's where you drink. I don't know how the marines ever got something like that. But anyhow, he would come in with us.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Captain, you know. We're not even used to P.F.C.'s smiling at us. And -- but I didn't drink. I didn't have a drink until I got overseas. Anyhow, so we graduated and then we had rubber boat landings and scouting and recon and all that. And then when we were finished we went aboard ship and overseas.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Tell me where you went from there then.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: We went to Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Camp Catlan(ph).

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: And right next to Honolulu. And they told us -- he says, "We've got open gate liberty." All you've got to do is show your I.D. card, because you was on the island of Hawaii and you're not going to swim back to the States, you know. But anyhow -- and, of course, before we got our liberty and all of that, they took us and they showed us a film on hygiene, on communicable diseases, you know. Do you think a marine would do that?

Anyhow -- and they said if you're caught in a house of ill repute, you will be tried and court marshalled. So I just turned seventeen, so, you know, I'm going to do what they tell me to do. But anyhow, so we got in and, of course, usually in groups. Because we had been together a few months, you know. We were buddy, buddies. And anyhow, so all they had -- it was so crowded with servicemen, all they had was curb to curb swabbies, Navy guys. Good outfit. So we was walking around, we saw the sergeant and we saw a line of marines, swabbies, doggies -- army guys -- waiting in line.

About every fifteen feet there was an M.P., military policeman or a shore patrol, Navy guy, thumping these guys, you know, for trying to break in line and all of that. So we ask -- the sergeant says, "What's going on there?" And he says, "Oh, that's the line in for the cat house." We said, "We were told we would get court marshalled." He said, "Well, it's good advice, kid." We never went in one.

But after two or three liberties if you went in to get a drink, they were watered down and they would give you only so many minutes to drink it. And if you didn't -- didn't leave by then, they would call the M.P. and they would throw you out. And food was -- you didn't think about buying food. It was three to four times it's regular price, you know, if they had it. So we stayed in. They had a big Red Cross building there. It was big. And they was real nice to us. And so I went in there and going to write home to mom and dad, you know, and the girlfriend I went to high school with and all that kind of stuff, you know. You know, pure white marine, you know. I ain't done anything.

But anyhow, so I was sitting there and I was kind of down, you know. And so this lady, and I would say in her middle thirties, early forties, very attractive Red Cross lady came in and she said, "Young man, you're down in the dumps." I said, "Yes, I am." And she said, "It must be tough to be overseas." I said, "Yes, it is." She said, "How long have you been overseas?" And I said, "Week and a half." And then from there, why -- this, what they call a draft, that's the number of men -- or that's the contingent of marines, and you get on the ship, you know, and then they take you over. And when we got to Pearl Harbor, half of -- there was about a thousand of us on board ship. Well, they said half of you will go to the 5th Amphib Corps, in which the 5th Marine Division was right there getting ready to go to Iwo Jima.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: And then he said the other of you will go to the 1st Marine Division.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: And that was you?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: That was me, yeah.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Because my initials.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: to R went to the 1st Marine Division or the 6th Marine Division. And then from S to Z went to the 5th Marine Division or the 3rd or 4th Division. But since the 5th Marine Division was right there in the Hawaiian Islands, that's where you went. We all wanted to go there because it was still Hawaii it seemed. So we went on board ship, and we went to the New Hebrides, which is a beautiful island. And we had to pick up some supplies, things like that, and some Aussies and -- we call them diggers.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: The Australians?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Yeah. Why, I don't know. Men from Australia. And then the New Zealanders and then they had a beer line. Well, I still hadn't drank beer yet. So every time they would have beer lines the guys would want to get next to me and say, "Hey Bud, remember me, your buddy, Flack, I did this for you and all of that," you know. So I would drink two Cokes -- I would take two beers and swap for Cokes, see. And -- so anyhow, so I -- then we got back on board ship. We did that in one day. And then we went to Guadalcanal and then to Island of Pavuvu, which sounds like a tropical disease and has been known to be. Anyhow, so we -- that's when things got serious.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: That's when you saw combat?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Yes. We was there and we stayed there several months. And -- uh, they had rats bigger than dogs and they had crabs about twelve inches in diameter. And at night, when they're crawling through the bushes, you think they're Japs and you shoot at them and all that. And then I found out the -- I started to drink -- well, on the way to the small boat from Guadalcanal to Pavuvu I had my first cigarette. And we was on this smaller ship and this gunnery sergeant says, "Okay, light them up," you know. Smoke _____+ well, I didn't light up. And he looked at me and he said, "Hey, Kid, do you smoke?" I said, "No, sir." He said, "Well, you're joining a combat outfit. They're old timers. They don't like sissies over there." He gave me a cigarette and then he lit it for me and I coughed and choked and when he wasn't looking I would flip it. But then I succumbed and all that.

And then we had -- every company -- we had five companies. 8AB -- four line companies and an H and S Company, which does radios and stuff like that. So but, hey, we learned that -- how to make home brew. And we had a guy in our draft that came over with us _________ six foot five Swede who got through high school and college by herding sheep in the south -- in the Dakotas. A very intelligent man. But he knew -- he learned how to make moonshine when he was a kid. When he was up in the winter time they did what they called wintering the sheep and you've got to take care of them. So there's nothing to drink up there, so you make your own. Well, they found out he was good, see. So they warmed up to us.

But the other combat marines who just got back from Beliliou [Peleliu?] and they had sixty, seventy percent losses. So we go into -- a platoon sergeant says, "Flack, there's your empty bunk." I threw my sea bag on it. These guys would throw my sea bag out and threw me out. Of course, that was one of those guys that was killed. So the -- then the sergeant came back and said, "Hey, we all did what this marine _________+. He's new and all that." He said, "Take care of him." So they warmed up to us, but they wouldn't speak to us and all that, you know, to a degree.

But when we got to -- on maneuvers and all that, and we let them know three months training, we knew what we were doing and they kind of warmed up to us. And then when we went on board the L.S.T, why we had -- a couple of nights before we had a beer party out of this world. That beer was stacked larger than this room. And my sergeant said, he says -- they called me chick or kid. And he said, "Kid?" I said, "Yeah, Sarge." I found out I didn't have to "sir-him" because he wasn't an officer. And he said you know the Japs could come in here _______+ and take this island back. Everybody is drunk. Well, we were, too. Well, the next day, though, we went on board ship on the L.S.T. and they took our amtrack in first and then we was loaded down with a couple of tons of explosives and all that and we packed it in.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: How many days had you been there at that point?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: From October -- well, of course, we stopped -- I would say several months.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Then we dogged them down -- or our amtrack and then we had amphibian tanks next to us, which is five, ten pounds heavier. They had cannons. We just have machine guns.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: And they dogged them down with, you know, hooks and they hooked in. Anyhow, so after we got all hooked in and all that stuff -- and so the crew chief, Blackie, Black Moll, M-O-L-L -- anyhow, why he said, "Flack get under the amtrack and check it. We've been over some maneuvers and we hit corral and all that, see how it looks." I said, "They got grease, oil, water, sun." He says make a move. And I had -- (Another tape had to be turned.)

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Okay. Anyhow, so I crawl back and all that. Well, when we backed in, we backed up against a big stack that had -- we didn't know what it was, but it was square as this, but about four foot taller. It was about twelve -- twelve foot. And it had a Navy century [sentry?] on it with an automatic rifle or a semi-automatic rifle. It must be something secret. You know, who cares. So when I crawled all the way back, that tarpaulin didn't come all the way down. What did I see before me, beer, cans of beer. Well, I pulled out my K-bar. A K-bar in the Marine Corps is a combat knife about this long and it just cuts. So here I am with my trusty combat knife like I'm going to find a Jap under, but I, like this, you know, and I cut out and I pull one out and I pop -- punctured it. And while I was checking it, boy, I drank that whole can, you know.

And then I thought -- and then Black is saying, "What are you doing under there, Kid? Get out of here." So I -- see, there was four of us in our crew, so I put four in my jacket and come out. And he says, "My, God, your dirty and all that. You ain't going to be a good marine." I wanted to say you're the one that put me under there, but you don't say that. He said, "What took you so long?" And I said ____________ the amtrack." So there was four of us, see. Three of us boots, we were all machine gunners and drivers and then the crew chief.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: We got there and I said, "Look what I got, beer." And they was like -- you know. So we drank the beer, you know. So anyhow, but we said, "Boy, we can get all the beer we want," you know. Well, after we got out to sea every evening, every evening chow, which is about 4:00 or 5:00, the swabbies give you a can of beer and they puncture it and give it to you.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: The swabbies are the Navy men?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Navy. I shouldn't call them that.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: No, no. That's good.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: I've got all the respect in the world for swabbies.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: This is all an education.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: So anyhow, but then a couple of days later, why a couple of sailors told us, says, "Hey, how you like the beer, jar heads?" That's another nickname. Jungle bunnies, for marines. And we said, "Oh, thanks a lot. We like it." He says, "We get all the beer we want. You jar heads get one a day until we get halfway there." He said, "Now, what are you going to do about that?" I tell you what we're going to do, so I told Blackie and Blackie says okay, we're going to get beer. So I go under there and bring it out, you know, and nobody knew what we was doing because that stack was leaning against our amtrack, which is back there it's about eight to ten foot tall and we had two tons of ammunition, so it's not going to move it.

And so we just passed out beer for our buddies and even a couple of swabbies we took a liking to. You always make friends with a swabbie that's in the galley. That's where the food is, or in the quarter master or in the Navy Corps man, in case you needed aspirins or whatever, you know. You learn. You still learn how to stay alive.

But anyhow, so the next thing I knew I -- they had on the -- they said in fifteen minutes the Master of Arms, which is the military police for the Navy, is going to come down and search all the amtracks and all the tanks. He says we can smell booze on your guys' breath at noon, you know. Well, we had about four or five cans that we hadn't started yet, but a 105 shell, which is about this long, about this big around, and it fits in a big tube. And so we took about two or three of these tubes, hard _______ tubes, they had a cap on it. And we put the ammunition right there on the ramp there where -- our machine gun ramp, and then we put all the beer in them and popped that.

And then when they come around to inspect us, why -- Leslie Milton Fall, our boot leader, he had a B.A. and a master's degree, but he was an old Dakota boy down in the heart. He was married, 28-years-old, with two kids and a wife. Anyhow, so I said, "What are we going to do?" And Slim, six foot five _____, he takes a cloth. He said, "All right, come on. Let's polish this brass. All four of you, shut up and polish. Here they come." So we was polishing the brass, you know, and they looked and they couldn't find anything. And they said, "What are you guys polishing the brass for?" And old Slim Fall says, "Haven't you ever heard of polishing brass?" And he said, "Yeah, what's it do?" He says, "This shell will go faster and more accurate when they shoot it if it's polished." And this Master of Arms had a couple of Navy seaman with him taking notes. And this Master of Arms says, "Make a note of that and all of our gun crews will start polishing the ammunition." Two Navy swabbies looking at us like, "You're dead meat, Boy." But we got away with it. So anyhow --

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: So that's sort of how you prepared for combat, huh?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Yeah. But something that has never, never left me was the night before -- or the -- we meet the beach head, and they had already shown us maps and things and all that and we knew where things were to be if we ever got in. And we woke up about -- well, nobody slept the night before. Let's see, we woke up and I had church. We only had one chaplain, so he handled all three faiths. And one thing I want to put in that I have learned or I've had to put up with after in the recent years was the different races not getting along, which is rather prevalent today. When I was in the Marine Corps we had all faiths, all nationalities. Nobody, but nobody ever, ever, ever made a difference. And anyhow, so we did that. And then we went down, we had chow. We had steak and eggs, coffee, toast, orange juice. And then we went to get ready to go up at boat(ph). And all -- everybody would say the doomed men get a hearty meal. But, you know -- but I was so scared. I have not been that frightened in my entire life. And so we got on and I was on the machine gun, fifty caliber machine gun. That was my favorite weapon. I was fortunate to do something pretty good with it. Anyhow --

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: How close were you to combat? Right there? How close was the enemy?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: You mean on the ship?

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Oh, we were several thousand yards out.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Because if we was close the Jap artillery would sink our ship.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: I see. Okay.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: So we came off the ship and I came out, you know, and all I could see was cruisers firing over our heads and -- just like in the movies, you know. And every time a ship would be behind firing you had to stay down because that blast of that, if you were standing up, or you was exposed, it would just blow you right out in the water.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: So you were manning the guns?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Well, we had three machine guns. We had three machine gunners and -- well, we had three recruits and our experienced. And he would man the machine gun if necessary and then one boot drove and the other of us two boots was on the machine guns. And -- so we had to go out there and _______ circles. And then when it come time for the third wave to go in, which wasn't too long, they would go in. And the airplanes would come down and dropping napalm. It was the whole nine yards. And I never -- you know, I was just seventeen years old. I should have been in my junior class at Broad Ripple. But, hey, you didn't have time to be afraid. Everything kicked in that you had been taught and that you had experienced that was going to keep you alive. But I still had fear. But fear is healthy. Fear is respect. But anyhow, we went in the third -- well, the first wave went in -- well, the zero wave went in. That's the armoured amphibian tanks. They just blew everything up. Then the first wave went in with machine guns and they tore everything up. And the second went in, the second wave went in, we was about four, five minutes apart, if that. Anyhow, so -- anyhow, by the time we got there, there was no targets because there wasn't but about a half dozen Japs.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: And this was the battle that took about an hour and a half you say?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Oh, no. This battle -- the overall battle?

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Well, you said --

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Three months.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay. There was one battle you said you thought was going to take three days and it took an hour and a half. That was later. The airport maybe you said?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Oh, yes, the airport. Yes, I'm sorry. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: I was getting ahead, right?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: No, you're doing fine. You're young. You have a more crisper memory than I do.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: But anyhow, like we say, we unloaded our ammunition and went over and helped them take these and stayed with the infantry and brought wounded back or and then we came back and then they put us on guard and machine gun nest and all that. Well, the third night -- no, I'm ahead of myself. The morning of the third day on the beach the Japs came over and striked us and bombed us about once every four to five hours.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: And so we dug slit trenches. Our platoon sergeant, you know, said do the slit trenches. And one of the guys said, "Well, can we get under our amtrack? It's made of steel." He says, "You've got a hundred and ten gallons of gas. If it's hit, you're burned to death." And every time we would have a condition red, which means air raid, you would see, everyone of us was ________. On the third day he did that, he didn't get back in, in time. The Japs scraped him and took part of his leg off. And boy he was a brilliant sergeant.

But anyhow, but that night also, about fifty Japs, a platoon of Japs came in with rubber boats in behind us and we didn't hear them because no engine or anything. They were paddling. Well, the Navy saw them and they hit the light on them, so we hit our light on them. We didn't have too many flares. But they was about fifty yards up from where I was and so our sergeant or acting platoon sergeant after that says, "Hold where you are. The guys are doing fine. If they need help, we'll help them." Because there may be some come in where we're at. And, well, the battle lasted about half an hour or forty-five minutes, if that. And we got one or two wounded. And there was about five got through -- got through us. And the wounded Japs, the only reason they surrendered because they wasn't strong enough to commit hara-kiri, which we would help them.

But you needed information and they said they was going over the Yontan Airfield. So on the radio system we told them, we says, "You've got at least a half dozen Japs coming over." And so about half an hour later we heard them cut loose over there. And they said they got all but one.

And then a couple of days later we was on our machine gun positions and here comes a Jap about fifty yards from us. And the guy next to me shot at him and hit him in the elbow and he went down. Then he came up again and the rifleman next to me shot him and killed him. So that was my first actual killing.

And then after a week and a half there we went across the island and they had four islands -- small islands over there and the Japs had radar and radio on it and they wanted to have it taken. And so we got a couple of companies out of the 5th -- out of the 5th Marines, and we went across the island and they met us there and we went in. It took us four days to take four of them, four of the islands. And took that without too much problem.

And came back and then on the way back we was going to patrol the coast of Okinawa because the Japs are coming in, see. And we could go on land and water, and we got three machine guns. So we did pretty good on that, but I remember when we was up and down the beach there and we ran into an army and it was holding some kind of a service. And so we stopped and said what's up. He says President Roosevelt just died. So the -- our commanding officer, "Okay, Marines out." So we got out and he gets us in formation. He said, "It's okay to bow our heads." We did.

And then we got back on our amtracks and got on with the war. And then around the 1st of May, why, the whole 1st division, we had the center part. We went down to relieve some Army divisions because they were really hit. I mean, they got -- they really got cut up bad. And so the 1st and 6th Marine Divisions, we went down -- we always stayed near the coast because we were amphibious. And that was May the 3rd. That night some Japs came in on us. We had two divisions there. And they had two battalions, about two battalions, about twelve hundred, and they landed separately, about fifteen minutes apart and we pretty well took care of them. And then we -- well, we took one prisoner. It was five hundred that hit close where we were at. He was wounded real bad and he couldn't kill himself, and that's the only one out of five hundred that was alive.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Out of the Japanese?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Of the Japanese, in our area. But right next to us, they did basically the same thing. And they got a couple of Jap prisoners. And, of course, if you go to take them, they kill themselves. If they're wounded, you go to help them and you pull them over and they got hand grenades under them. They booby-trap themselves. So tough toenails. And this one that we got, we got up and tied a rope around his ankle and got back about fifty feet and drug him and then flipped him over and he was -- he never had a chance to kill himself. But anyhow, they talked and they said -- they was about four miles -- they was supposed to hit four miles up from us, not where we were, see. Anyhow, so that was taken care of.

And then two days later we headed down to the front lines and it was on a Sunday and -- so we went on down and relieved the Army and they were cut up real bad. And so we took our amtracks and we would stay with certain battalions and companies, you know. When they would make an attack, we would be right with them with our armour and machine guns and stretchers. And we did that, you know. And then at night, the amtracks would either -- we would be assigned. Half of the amtracks would be on the front lines down below the crest so the enemy can't see you. And then, of course, we had three machine guns and we would lend them our machine guns if they needed it. And then the other bunch would -- we would -- they had forward aid stations that are about five hundred yards, four hundred yards from the front lines. And the Japs at night would infiltrate and bayonet the wounded and throw hand grenades at them. So we would take a couple of amtracks with the infantry and we would guard our wounded buddies.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: So -- but anyhow, I --

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Is that where you were wounded as well?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Yes. I was wounded -- I found out I -- it was the third Sunday or the last Sunday of May. And the only reason I knew it was a Sunday because early in the morning my buddy and I had -- (END OF TAPE NUMBER 1, SIDE 1) (BEGINNING OF TAPE 1, SIDE 2)

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: -- the third Sunday in May.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Third Sunday in May. Okay.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: The only reason we knew it was Sunday because we picked up the wounded and took them up to the regimental hospital, the tent hospital, and coming back a chaplain and his assistant had set up -- it had been raining for at least two weeks, two and a half weeks, and we was up to mud here. And that's the reason the amtracks -- they could mobilate, but even our amtrack that night got stuck. But anyhow, so we stopped a few minutes for the services, but we had to get on, you know. And during the day we did what we usually do; Help the infantry out on attacks. Or if an infantryman was wounded out in no-man's land and they couldn't _______+ machine gunners, we had half-inch armour. We would go right out, drop our ramp, put the wounded on, and I would be on the machine gun and fire back in case we got shot at. So we was pretty good buddies with the infantry. Well, we're all together.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Anyhow, so -- but we was in a battle for Wana Ridge. And that night it was just before dusk we were bringing down wounded and putting them on our amtrack and get them up to the forward aid station before it got dark. Well, due to the mud conditions and all that, we had two stretcher -- two stretcher patients and two or three walking wounded. And between all of us, we would take them down this high ridge. And one time one fell off of the -- one wounded fell off the stretcher and rolled down and we got him. We found it easier just one man take his legs, somebody take his arms.

But anyhow, by the time we got them loaded and secured in our amtrack, it was dark. And so as the marines -- the other marines had helped, had started to go back up and they said, "Hey, guys, you know don't move at night." Anybody that -- anybody that moves at night is going to be -- you kill them, no matter what. So we didn't know to do that. So we started out. We knew we had to get going and take the risk, and we bogged down in mud. And so I knew where the forward aid station was, so I told my buddy Griff -- we was only two of us left.

The first week and a half we lost -- we lost Fall, Rusty Nolton Fall and lost our crew chief. And so there was just two of us. Never been in combat before. And the acting platoon sergeant said, "That's all right, Kid." He said, "I'll have you two more replacements." I'm still waiting. Anyhow, so I went over the side and I was armed with a Thompson sub-machine gun and I was just holding some grenades. And when the flares would come up, I would go down on -- real flat. And then when they would burn out -- I had already picked out a place about fifty, seventy-five feet from me, when it was dark I would take off for that.

Well, I was taking off, I had went about a hundred fifty, two hundred yards and I was crossing a roadbed and I sunked down to my knees. Anyhow, up come the flare and I saw two figures. I started to shoot them, but we was behind our own lines. They should have been our marines, but I didn't know. And all of a sudden one started shooting at me and the other threw a grenade and I fired back.

Whether I hit one or not, I don't know. But the grenade exploded behind me. It went down in the mud, that's what saved me. But still got in the arms and all that stuff in my back. And I didn't feel pain, but I felt stinging and burning when I was hit with the fragments. And I made it on and on. And I had a piece there in the back of my hand.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: And you were carrying wounded as well, right?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: No, no. The wounded -- no, the wounded were on the amtrack. I was going to get another amtrack and bring it down.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Well, anyhow, to make a long story short, I'm taking up too long.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: That's all right.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: But anyhow, I went up and -- I knew where the forward aid station was. When I got thirty, forty foot from it, I -- as soon as the flare went up, I said, "Hey, wounded marine coming in." And they said, "What's the password?" Well, I couldn't remember the password because we was working for different battalions and things like that. And they said, "Well, what's your name, serial number, and platoon you went through in boot camp?" Well, they could tell whether you -- marines are sort of small in size. We could tell. I told him. And about that time one of my buddies says -- amtrack buddies says, "Hey, that's Johnny Flack." And he said, "I'll go out and get him." And the sergeant said, "Hold it." And my buddy said, "You know where you can go, buddy." So darted out and the flare was up and then another marine I never knew came out with him and they brought me in.

And while they was dressing my wounds I told Tim Gilson and Harry Hines, they were amtrack crew. And I told them what I had. And they said okay. And the corps man said, "I'm going to give you a shot," you know. And I said, "No, I've got to keep my head clear." And, of course, my marine buddy said, "That will be the day."

But anyhow, so they helped me on the amtrack and I was -- and we went through -- we got pinged at a couple of times and we found our buddy, my amtrack, and went in there like that and they put a one-inch cable and got it out. It came up. And so then the Corps man, he -- in the arm and all. So I go in the corner and I sacked out till about 6:00 in the morning, 7:00. About 6:00 or 7:00, whatever it was. They work everybody else, you know. And after he gave me a shot, he didn't put it all in me. So he took my lapel, my jacket -- he took the -- it had a little cap on it. And it's a little tube about this big, like a metal tube about this big, about this thick, about that wide, and he run it through my collar and then he screwed the cap on. He said, "Now, if you get hurting, just take it out and -- like this."

And anyhow, so then he said ______ we've got a truck up here and we're going to haul all you wounded back up there to the, you know, regimental camp hospital. And so about that time my buddy shows up in the amtrack and my lieutenant shows up in an amtrack. And my lieutenant comes up and said, "I tried to make it sooner, John, but we couldn't move at night." And I said, "I know," and all that. And so -- I looked at him and all that and I said, "Hey," I took that tag, like that, and I said, "I'm staying." And my lieutenant said, "You don't have to." I said, "I know I don't have to, but there's guys hurt worse than me that's fighting out there." He said, "That's okay, Johnny." He said -- I had a wonderful lieutenant, a good leader. And he said, "It only takes one hand to fire a machine gun. Just swap your arm ______+. So -- and he gave us some rations and we took off. And every time I'd see a different corps man they would change -- and then went on and -- basically the same thing until the campaign was over.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: On other same island there?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: We -- well, the island was declared secured on the 22nd of June, but we stayed down till June the 30th because the Japs had pockets that were still fighting. So they told me, "Flack, you and your platoon was going to be" -- not my platoon. He said, "Your platoon is going to help us out." And I said, "Okay." But anyhow --

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: We came back up to the encampment. We stayed on Okinawa. And, of course, they gave us a couple -- a week or so off, you know, to get laundry and things like that and get your weapons taken care of and get new machine gun barrels and all that. And then we got down to the business of getting ready to engage -- invade Japan. And the way we found out about the atom bomb, every morning you had reveille and then you get ready and then you go and have chow and then you have muster. And then after muster you go and check the bulletin board to see what kind of duties you got that day. Like guard duty, mess duty, or whatever, you know. So while we were checking that, of course, Sergeant Gross came out. He's our Company First Sergeant, finest first sergeant I ever knew. And so he put a bulletin up there and it said -- this was in August. And he said a bomber dropped an atom bomb, which has explosive power of twenty thousand tons, through a Japanese city. I don't know if they said Hiroshima or not. And we said that's superman stuff. That's comic book stuff, you know. An airplane carry a twenty thousand ton bomb, get out of here.

So we went about our business, you know. They spelled the atom was, A-T-O-M. We didn't know what an atom was. Now, Slim did, but he had a tough time, you know, trying to explain it to us. He said, "You guys are too thick." How true. Well, a few days later another bomb was dropped, and we did the same thing. And when they got through with that bulletin he just tossed it. You know, but anyhow, the next thing we knew there was rumors of peace. And then the day before VJ-Day they called us all out, you know. And our battalion commander colonel called us out and he says -- talked to the company commander. And he thanked us and all that and stuff. You know, he was a ______ colonel. Anyhow -- and then we broke down to companies and then from companies down to platoons. And Lieutenant Noreen our lieutenant, he had us get in a circle -- get in a circle and hold hands. Marines don't hold hands, but we did.

He said bow your heads, men. And we all prayed. Thank God. And then he said, "Okay. Now" -- he had a big satchel there and he opens it up and he had several bottles of whiskey. He says, "Okay, guys, down 'er." We said, "Sir, you drink first," because we respected him. He was like this, you know. But when things are just to a G.I., he could be a G.I. And if you fouled up, he chewed in a circle and let it drop out, but he never made you live with it. And then we was -- after that we was transferred to the 1st Tank Battalion because they didn't need beach heads anymore. And besides, a tank operates like an amtrack. So then from there we went to China.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: I didn't get to China at first. My buddies -- some of my buddies and I had very serious infections and jungle rot in our ears and all that, you know. And we had to -- every day we had to go to the _______ hospital and they would take care of us. And there was guys ________ going to China. They didn't have anything set up there for us, so a couple of weeks later when they set up, we went to China, tanks. And I was almost a year, eleven months and a half, overseas in China. And I went from assistant driver up to tank commander. Anyhow, but we was on patrol. We fought the Chinese communists. We were in Tianjin. And we had patrols -- you got anything you got to --

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: No, keep going.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: I'm just taking a couple of notes.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Okay. We would try to keep the railroad and bridges open between Peiping and Tianjin. And then a couple of times we went out almost to the outer rim of the Gobi Desert. We went a couple of times up to the Great Wall of China. The first time we saw it we said, "Wow." After that, we went up there another time we said, "What a waste." And -- but we like Peiping. And then they had a train school up there and we would guard the bridges. But when you wasn't doing your patrol duty, you packed with your tank battalion. If you volunteered to ride shotgun on these trains, you could spend two days liberty up in Peiping, because there wasn't too many Chinese communists up there and it was just liberty. And there wasn't no swabbies up there. When the Navy comes in, they've been at sea and they got three months pay and they inflate all the prices, you know. We would have to get rid of them, so -- anyhow, why --

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: So how long were you in China?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Till August '46.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Just a month less than a year.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Anyhow, why, I got in some problems and things like that. Around the first, second week of June we were getting a new two-star general. So we had the regimental review, that's six, seven thousand men, or close to that, whatever. That higher rank, I don't know. But, you know, and then you have the guys -- the infantry goes through in trucks, the artillery goes through, and motor transport and all that stuff and then the tanks are last. I was a tank commander. And I had a real good tank and I had the best crew in the platoon, you know. But we had a new lieutenant come in, never been in combat, and a new gunny sergeant, who had never been in tanks.

But after the war ended, we had a surplus of high rank, you know. And so this gunny sergeant, David Gray, I get my tank parked and all and he comes up and said, "You take that tank up there." I said, "Beg your pardon, Gunny." I said, "This is my tank I'm assigned to this and this is my crew. I've got the best." He said my five stripes -- I was a corporal. And I was up for sergeant. In fact, it had been okayed down here at the battalion. It had to go up to headquarters.

Well, I didn't want to make too much a fuss with him, but I said okay. And then they give me a driver that was not an experienced driver and the tank was a dog. It hadn't been maintenanced right, but I was going to see it through. So when the tanks went like this to -- they have the -- okay, here's the -- the viewing stand and here they had the _______ ran and we were supposed to go between them. And I'm in my tank and my turret, you know, like you see in the movies on up there like this, you know. So this kid that was driving didn't know how to start it, and by the time I got it, it got flooded. And by the time we got it started and everything got running right, the -- we were supposed to go around like this and then go between, the band and the stand.

So we was right here, so I said cut and go right in behind them. They'll never notice the difference. Well, we did that. He got it going too fast and the _______ flies and he hit the left brake too hard and a fan tail on the left side of the tank hit their unit stand and a two-star general went down with a Chinese squall.

And, boy, that lieutenant, when we got back to the tank park, he was screaming, the gunny was screaming. The lieutenant was so distraught he started actually crying, you know. I said, "The war is over. What have you got to worry about?" So he was going to put me up for a court martial, you know, negligence of duty and all that. And the first sergeant, First Sergeant Giletti, another fine guy, he says, "You're not going to do that with Flack. I've been with him a year here and we're going to promote him and hope he stays in the Marine Corps." And the lieutenant says here's my papers and everything. I want him court martialled.

That was my platoon. Anyhow, so the first sergeant said -- he said, "No, Lieutenant." The Lieutenant says, "See them bars. I'm an officer and you're not." And so the First Sergeant picks up the company roster, the First Sergeant is over the whole Company. And this Lieutenant is only over one of the four or five platoons.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: He said, "What are you over?" He said, "That platoon." And the First Sergeant said, "I'm over the whole Company." He took them papers and ripped them up and then -- of course, I never saw sergeant again. But anyhow, I went home. And the First Sergeant said, "If you stay, I'll guarantee you sergeant." No, I want to go home and see mom and dad.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: So you left China and went straight home?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Yeah, on the -- yeah. And some buddies of mine went. I don't know, I brought some stuff here.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Yeah, let me get that from you when we're done with the tape here.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: That's fine. So what did you do -- just to summarize a little bit, what did you do when you got home? What was your -- in the days and weeks when you --

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Well, I was going to sort of loaf and all that. And then they have what's called a 52-20 Club. I don't know whether you heard about it. In fact, I had it and I should have brought it. You go down to the ___________ and you get twenty dollars and you hunt for a job.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: And 52-20, you can get 52 twenty-dollar checks in a year. And then I had three hundred dollars mustering out pay, a hundred dollars when I was mustered out from Chicago. And then when I got home -- get to Great Lakes. And then two months later. Oops, sorry about that.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Anyhow, this is the menu for Pavuvu in 1944. But anyhow --

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: What did you do then? What was your career after you came back?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Well, I laid out a week and all that and I said, "Hey, this is not for me." And I had quite a bit of money in the bank because when I was overseas I didn't spend money overseas. And then I bought a 25-dollar bond every third month.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: So I was in pretty good shape. Anyhow, I went to work a couple of places and I wasn't doing any good. My brother got me a job where he was working. The guy made wooden storm doors and windows. And he gives me the sander. I didn't know anything about a sander and I botched up everything I did. The man who owned the company is a good Christian man. He said, "John, I like you and all that, but you're costing me money." I said, "Okay." And he was a fine man. And I went to work a couple of other places and it just didn't work out. In fact, I was getting myself together to go back and re-enlist. And then I went to work for a dairy, Robert's Dairy. And then I liked that. And -- wonderful people to work for and work with and all that. And I really got myself into it. And then they started sending me to different schools and everything to learn about milk. Milk just doesn't come out of the cow and they put it in a bottle and take off with it. It has to be tested, it has to be pasteurized. Well, I learned all of that, and I went right up in rank, you know, for what it's worth. And then I got married on June 5, 1948.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Last week my wife and I were married fifty-four years. Anyhow, so I'm doing fine and all of that, but just getting ready to -- we didn't have any children yet. And we were getting ready to prepare to have children and all that. Our first four years we went out and drank and boozed, but had a good time. And I was never a heavy boozer. I very seldom ever smoked. After I left the Marine Corps I -- when you're in the Marine Corps and you're in combat, the only thing that keeps you going is a cup of coffee and a cigarette. But such wasn't the same here. But anyhow, that was it.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Okay. I'm going to -- on your military awards you got the Purple Heart Medal, The Combat Action Ribbon.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Two, yeah.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Two.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: That's all right. One is enough.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Marine Corps Reserve Medal, American Campaign Medal, Adriatic Pacific Campaign Medal with two battle stars, World War II Victory Medal, Navy Occupation Medal with the Adriatic clasp, the China Service Medal, National Defense Service Medal, China War Memorial Medal.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Yeah, that was sent to me in 1991 from Washington D.C. through the Chinese Consulate. Every marine that worked in that got one, so I'm not anything exceptional.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Korean Service Medal with two Battle Stars. United Nations Service Medal, Presidential Unit Citation with one Battle Star Okinawa, and Republic of Korea Presidential Unit Citation. Do you want to make any comment about your military awards?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: No. Except for the Purple Heart, everybody gets one. So that's the best thing I can say. No, that's about it. I was surprised to get the China Commemorative Medal and -- but anyhow, why, they start sending them -- you had to write in and had to have your documentation, which is not hard to get. I mean, if you've got them, you've got them. Anyhow, and -- but I called up and, like I say, I was in amtracks and tanks, which is -- the M.O.S. is armoured track. And so I went in and we were put in the infantry. I was a squad leader. But it was more not so much for teaching tactics, infantry tactics because I had never been in the infantry before. But it was to get you physically prepared, mentally prepared, and things like that. And then I did six weeks, a couple of months of that, and then I was sent over to the amtrack school. It was called Camp Delmar then. They finally found out I was an amtracker and then the tanks was right next to them, so I could be either one. I did that a couple of weeks and then over I went. And then -- so --

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: To summarize, could you tell us how -- just how you -- you know, you were so young when you joined, how did that experience in the service, how did that affect the rest of your life and your life experiences?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: I grew up. Being a marine you learned to be a leader. You learn to be positive, objective. That's -- I would say that's one of the most important things there is. You learn to get along with people. You learn to take care of your buddies and your buddies take care of you. No marine has ever let another marine down, in the field of battle or anywhere else. But with Korea I went part of the -- the last part of one campaign into another and then I came home in April. But I never did anything spectacular except stay alive, but I -- it helped me, because when I got back I went back to the dairy and so they was very kind to me. I went on a milk route, which paid double what I was making.

And so -- but you had to go out to earn -- work it, but it was very good. Anyhow, but I looked around after about four or five years. We had our first son in '52, our second son in '54, ten years later we had our daughter. We wasn't trying for that, but it was -- you talk about a gift from God. Anyhow, I so -- but I saw a lot of those fire -- fireman -- those milkmen in and out a couple hundred times a day, day in and year out and all that, they were in bad shape. So I said I've got to get out of this. And so I joined the police department. And I stayed 35 years. I went from patrolman up to captain. And the captain was a temporary rank. At that time that I made it the chief we had was an interim chief, didn't believe in permanent ranks. And I lasted four years and they took it to court -- there was about thirty of us promoted -- twenty of us, I'm sorry. And one of the guys took it to court to get it permanent and the judge backed the chief up and all of our promotions were taken away from us because it was temporary. That's neither here nor there.

I liked being a lieutenant anyhow. But I was a lieutenant for -- I made lieutenant in '69. And in between I made captain, which I didn't really like anyhow, because you were behind a desk with two secretaries. But I received several awards and things like that. I was injured fourteen times. And during my time as a police officer, 35 years, eighteen officers were killed in Indianapolis, four of them were mine. I was with three of them as they died and one I wasn't. It was my night off. But he lived nine days and I would go up to the hospital every morning. And every time a policeman dies, just like in the Marine Corps, a part of you goes with them.

And I've been fortunate to receive some awards. 38 commendations, valor eight times, Policeman of the Year. I was put in the Red Cross Hall of Fame in Washington, D.C. for valor. But anything a policeman does is just about bravery or valor. There's a difference. One or the other. And out of that I spent two years with the -- well, I went to three narcotic schools, national schools, and then I was put on leave of absence from the Indianapolis Police Department and sworn into Department of Justice. And I was there almost two years when I was injured pretty seriously. I had to come out. But I was in command of a six to eight, nine-man teams. And our mission was to infiltrate and take off heroin and cocaine traffickers throughout the middle west, which we did.

I had 32 investigations, 32 arrests and 31 convictions. The one conviction I didn't get, they put in a temporary judge, they're called -- I forget the name of them. And the judge, the one that -- ordered me to name and bring forth the informant that gave us information that we had for that arrest. And I said "No, I can't do that. He'll be dead meat." He said, "That's an order or it's dismissed." I said, "You're the judge, and I will not do it." Okay. He put the guy out. Of course, the guy got killed about six months later by a pusher, another pusher, so God works in mysterious ways. But anyhow --

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Well, let's wrap up as far as the veterans stuff.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: No, no, you've been wonderful. Just to summarize is there anything that you want to tell me about your -- about your service in the war that we haven't covered?

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Yes. The most meaningful or the happening that really, really hit me was when my brother was killed in the Navy and he was killed November of '42. I was still a freshman in high school. And I didn't -- well, my dad and mother always got up around 6:00 and prepared -- I had ______ and stuff. And I had four brothers then besides me, five of us. I had two brothers in the Navy, one in the Air Force, and one in the Army infantry. Anyhow, we was getting ready to get up and I could hear my father shout and my mother scream. And, of course, we all come running down. And it was a telegram that was lodged between the storm door and the door. And my dad went to get the Morning Star and there was that telegram. He opened it up and it stated that your son had been killed in action. It wasn't delivered or knocked on the door or anything and we never knew why.

And, of course, the other happening that stayed with me was the _______. Later on we found out how they acted in the States, which we had been there we might have, too. ______+ and everything and all that. And -- but anyhow, overseas in combat, my grammar is terrible -- but anyhow -- anyhow, when it happened we were stunned. We didn't -- you know, we were stunned. We couldn't believe it. And even when they announced it to us and all that and we got together. Well, after the lieutenant, we downed a couple of bottles and all that and shook hands with him and he went back to what he was doing and they gave us several days off. We went back to our tents, made coffee, and we always managed to get little tins about this big around, about that high of ham -- ham salad or whatever, and we always had crackers. So that's what we would have in the evening.

And we would sit there -- nobody drank anymore, but we sat there and talked to each other. Tears, yeah. And ____________ talking to them who survived combat. We just couldn't believe it. But we knew one thing, we were going home not in a casket, but to see our loved ones. And then the big thing, the ones we lost and all. You know, why didn't they live. Well, I believe that God has a lot to do with that. And anyhow -- and then when I became a Christian -- I didn't have the Lord as my saviour until 1969 when I was a policeman, a lieutenant. And that one night, why, I was on the late shift and I saw -- I always worked the inner city, about eighty percent. And there was a three story tenement blazing. So I got on the radio to headquarters, I said, "Get the fire department out here." And my sergeant hit on the radio, he said, "I'm on the way." And then he told different units to be there. He knew what to do and all that, you know.

And we handled the traffic and all that. The main thing was people trapped in it. So anyhow, the fire department still hadn't got there and hadn't set up. So I went to the back of the apartment and one of my men said -- no, a guy leaned out the window and said there's two trapped up here and one upstairs, the third floor, a three-year-old girl. So the one guy made it out, but this other guy couldn't, so he jumped out of a two-story building and landed on the concrete. So -- and then about that time the heat was so bad that it blew the windows out, shattered. So the guys held a blanket over my head and he had two broken ankles, compound, the bones were out. So I had to set both of those in order to move him. And, of course, the consequence of that, you know, if you moved him and those bones moved, they might cut vessels, arteries, veins. And so we got him out and then I ran around and I headed up to the third floor and I got driven back by the smoke. So I came down to the second floor -- they had balconies. So my men, I said, "Throw me my gas mask."

And they throwed it to me, I put it on, and I went up inside. And I couldn't find the girl. And then I found out that the -- it used to be one apartment, now it's two. And they had the -- the hallway was blocked off. This is what you call your slum landlords and why people die. So I came back down. I went to the front and went up. When I got up to the third floor, some firemen was following me up. And just as I got almost to the third floor the whole -- the floors and everything just blew like that. So it hit me and I went tumbling down the steps, unconscious.

A fireman grabbed me. This one captain grabbed me and carried me down onto the street. They got to put me on a stretcher, threw me in ambulance and took me out to Wishard Hospital, and I was unconscious for an hour, hour and a half. And there's no antidote for smoke and heat inhalation. You live or you die.

Well, fortunately when I left the Marines in '51, I never, ever smoked another cigarette. And, you know, they taste bad and all of that, that was enough of that. So anyhow, so finally I came around and about 4:00 in the morning I left the hospital and I drove up to where this fire was because I lost my flashlight. It was _______ that my kids had bought me for birthday. I couldn't find it and I was going through the -- all that stuff. And an elderly black man come over. We were in the black neighborhood. And he said, "You're a lieutenant, aren't you?" I said, "Yes, sir, I am." He said, "You know, the brass come back when the tough stuff is over." I said, "Whatever you say."

Well, I was going to church. See, my wife and I was going to church. East 91st Street Christian Church. And the Reverend Blowers, you know, I wasn't baptized, because I'm going to nail you. I said there ain't no way. Because everything that I did, I did because I was who I was and how I was trained and all that good garbage. So anyhow, so we went to church and then after each sermon -- after it's over with they play that little music come forward, you know, da-da. Something got ahold of me, stood me up and my wife next to me, and I started up. Boy, she grabbed my arm and up with me, you know. Reverend Blowers said, "Hold the music, hold it." The walls are going to cave in, John Flack is up there. So we shook hands and we made, you know -- and then during the week we went to his office, you know, to make sure I wasn't just making a grandstand in there. And so when Sunday, the next Sunday, they baptized my wife and I and they put on the white sheet over me, you know, and then -- and I told my minister, I said, "You was holding me under about two minutes more than my wife." So there was a good way I met him, but you've got other priorities, so anyhow.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: No. Well, we'll wrap up the tape then and, Mr. Flack, I really appreciate you sharing your story with us.

sp.speaker: John H. Flack
sp.p: Well, it's my privilege.

sp.speaker: Gail Lowry
sp.p: Thank you.
[Conclusion of interview]
